name: Make It Ascending
description: You are given an array $$$a$$$ consisting of $$$n$$$ elements. You may apply several operations (possibly zero) to it. During each operation, you choose two indices $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ ($$$1 \le i, j \le n$$$; $$$i \ne j$$$), increase $$$a_j$$$ by $$$a_i$$$, and remove the $$$i$$$-th element from the array (so the indices of all elements to the right to it decrease by $$$1$$$, and $$$n$$$ also decreases by $$$1$$$). Your goal is to make the array $$$a$$$ strictly ascending. That is, the condition $$$a_1 \lt a_2 \lt \dots \lt a_n$$$ should hold (where $$$n$$$ is the resulting size of the array). Calculate the minimum number of actions required to make the array strictly ascending.
input_specification: The first line contains one integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1 \le T \le 10000$$$) — the number of test cases. Each test case consists of two lines. The first line contains one integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 15$$$) — the number of elements in the initial array $$$a$$$. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1$$$, $$$a_2$$$, ..., $$$a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 10^6$$$). It is guaranteed that: the number of test cases having $$$n \ge 5$$$ is not greater than $$$5000$$$; the number of test cases having $$$n \ge 8$$$ is not greater than $$$500$$$; the number of test cases having $$$n \ge 10$$$ is not greater than $$$100$$$; the number of test cases having $$$n \ge 11$$$ is not greater than $$$50$$$; the number of test cases having $$$n \ge 12$$$ is not greater than $$$25$$$; the number of test cases having $$$n \ge 13$$$ is not greater than $$$10$$$; the number of test cases having $$$n \ge 14$$$ is not greater than $$$3$$$; the number of test cases having $$$n \ge 15$$$ is not greater than $$$1$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print the answer as follows: In the first line, print $$$k$$$ — the minimum number of operations you have to perform. Then print $$$k$$$ lines, each containing two indices $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ for the corresponding operation. Note that the numeration of elements in the array changes after removing elements from it. If there are multiple optimal sequences of operations, print any one of them.
approach_summary: Define state dp[mask][i] capturing the subset of visited/chosen elements. Transition by iterating over valid unset bits in O(2^N × N) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1342F — Make It Ascending [450. Bitmask DP]
topic_editorial.summary: Bitmask DP state compression over subsets.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because the dimension $N$ is small ($N \le 20$), each subset of chosen or visited elements can be encoded compactly into a single bitmask integer $0 \le \text{mask} < 2^N$. The optimal substructure property guarantees that to extend a subset $\text{mask}$, we only need to know the current subset and optionally the last added element.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: State Definition
Define $dp[\text{mask}]$ (or $dp[\text{mask}][u]$ if the last visited element matters) as:
- $dp[\text{mask}] = $ the optimal value obtainable using the subset of elements represented by the bitmask $\text{mask}$.

### Step 2: Base Cases
- Initialize all DP states to a sentinel value (e.g. $\infty$ for minimization, or $-\infty$ for maximization).
- Base state: $dp[0] = 0$ (empty configuration has cost zero).

### Step 3: Recurrence Relation & Transitions
For every mask from $0$ to $2^N - 1$:
If the state $dp[\text{mask}]$ is reachable:
For every element $i \in [0, N-1]$ such that the $i$-th bit is NOT set in $\text{mask}$ ($(\text{mask} \mathbin{\&} (1 \ll i)) == 0$):
$$\text{next\_mask} = \text{mask} \mid (1 \ll i)$$
$$dp[\text{next\_mask}] = \text{opt}\big(dp[\text{next\_mask}], dp[\text{mask}] + \text{cost}(\text{mask}, i)\big)$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
The final answer is stored in $dp[(1 \ll N) - 1]$, which corresponds to all $N$ elements being chosen.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N \cdot N)$
  There are $2^N$ total bitmasks. From each mask, we iterate over at most $N$ possible next bits to transition. For $N = 20$, $2^{20} \cdot 20 \approx 2 \times 10^7$ operations, which easily runs in $\approx 0.15$ seconds.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N)$
  Storing the DP table for all $2^N$ configurations requires $2^{20} \times 8$ bytes $\approx 8\text{ MB}$ of memory, well below 256 MB.
